item.title: Anthropic warns AI models may soon self-replicate and could wreak havoc on the web
item.description: A new warning about artificial intelligence from Anthropic caused a stir in cybersecurity circles on Tuesday, a day after the company warned that AI models could be months away from self-replicating across the internet.
item.dc:creator: Raphael Satter, Harshita Varghese
item.content:encoded: A new warning about artificial intelligence from Anthropic caused a stir in cybersecurity circles on Tuesday, a day after the company warned that AI models could be months away from self-replicating across the internet. In a post late Monday, Anthropic raised the possibility that rogue AI could spin up a botnet, spread quickly, fight takedown attempts and even break into data centers to turbocharge its growth. Some experts said Tuesday that they shared the company's concern, although at least one said the company appeared to be engaging in "vendor exaggeration." Monday's post fleshed out a warning last month from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who floated the idea that within the next year or even sooner, AI might be able to hijack "the entire internet" with "a persistent botnet." Cybersecurity experts who pushed back on the doomsday scenario argued that models would be too big to move around efficiently and could not draw on enough computer power to operate independently. The post made an early attempt to articulate how those challenges could be overcome. The company said its experiments showed medium-sized AI models with 30 billion parameters or less could already perform many of the individual tasks required for self-replication, even if they struggled to complete the entire process reliably. Anthropic said the models could then stitch together the required compute by hijacking inexpensive internet-connected devices. It added that the models were able to replicate across a simplified test network. "A replicator like this would be challenging to shut down, since there's no centralized point to shut off," the company said. The report adds to broader concerns about the security risks tied to increasingly capable AI systems, including their potential to automate cyberattacks, operate with limited human oversight and circumvent safeguards. The advances in models have prompted a series of often dire warnings from industry heads and AI company employees about the possibility of severe, even existential, risks of runaway AI development. Some cybersecurity experts were skeptical. "'We managed to run a small model on cheap TVs,' does not a security crisis make," said Ciaran Martin, a former head of Britain's National Cyber Security Centre. He said the post came across as an "interesting technical paper with a more than hint of vendor exaggeration." Others expressed more concern. Zhengxiong Li, an assistant professor of computer science and engineering at the University of Colorado Denver, said that while the testing had been done in controlled conditions, he still found it worrying that an AI could effectively become a "worm," a self-replicating program that could improvise ways to hijack devices on the fly. "If it runs across many devices without depending on a central service, there may be no single place to shut it down," he said. Anthropic said that if smaller models continue improving at their historical rate, they could reach the capability required for autonomous replication by the end of 2026. It also floated the idea that the models might find ways to target more powerful computing resources, including data-center processors, that could potentially enable them to draw on much bigger pools of computer power. One researcher said it made sense to think of the Anthropic post as more of a hypothetical than a prediction. It made sense to consider the possibility of AI models proliferating autonomously given the past three months of revelations over rogue AI activity, said Jessica Ji, a senior research analyst at Georgetown’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology. But she said, "we don’t know yet what the likelihood of that actually happening is — it’s not zero, but nor is it guaranteed."

item.title: Trump says he does not believe China and Russia help Iran, contradicting US intelligence
item.description: President Donald Trump said on Monday he did not believe that China and Russia were helping Iran "at all," even as US intelligence reports in recent months have found that both countries directly support Tehran's war effort.
item.dc:creator: Kanishka Singh, Erin Banco, Jonathan Landay
item.content:encoded: President Donald Trump said on Monday he did not believe that China and Russia were helping Iran "at all," even as US intelligence reports in recent months have found that both countries directly support Tehran's war effort. Trump said on Truth Social that he had seen comments from his critics and opponents that China and Russia were helping Iran. Moscow and Beijing maintain close ties with Tehran. "If they are, it's at a very low level, but I don't believe they are at all. They have too much to lose, and we would know about it, and know about it very fast," Trump wrote. U.S. intelligence assessments from recent months have shown that Russia and China are providing military support to Iran in the form of satellite imagery for targeting purposes and components for weapons, according to two people briefed on the matter. Trump said in July he [USN:L1N43Q0M0 TEXT:"trusted China and Russia"] not to help Tehran in the Iran war, but warned that if they did get involved "it would be very bad for them." The United States and Iran have been at war since February 28 when the US and Israel attacked Iran and Tehran responded with its own strikes on Israel and Gulf states that host US bases. US-Israeli strikes on Iran and Israeli attacks on Lebanon have since [USN:L1N3ZR14Q TEXT:"killed thousands"] and [USN:L6N3ZY0Q0 TEXT:"displaced millions"]. Trump has [USN:L6N42P16R TEXT:"previously described"] Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin as "neutral" during the Iran war. Russia has said the Iran war could [USN:S8N3Z908L TEXT:"lead to a nuclear arms race"] in the Middle East. Beijing has condemned Washington's attacks on Tehran as a brazen violation of Iran's sovereignty. Last month, Trump warned Xi against providing support to Iran when the Chinese leader visited Washington, and received assurances that China would not do so, the US ambassador to China said at the time. The warning came on the back of reports that China had supplied Iran with shoulder-fired air-defense missile launchers and that Tehran had found ways to evade sanctions on its oil sales with Chinese help. In September, Trump [USN:L8N4550G3 TEXT:"brushed aside"] a report that Iran acquired satellite images of a base in Jordan from Chinese entities before an attack that killed three US troops there in July.

item.title: Dollar retreats from 18-month high as oil prices fall, inflation data in focus
item.description: The dollar slipped from an 18-month high on Tuesday as oil prices retreated and investors reassessed the AI-fueled rally that has supported demand for US assets this year, while awaiting fresh clues on the Federal Reserve's interest rate path.
item.dc:creator: Laura Matthews
item.content:encoded: The dollar slipped from an 18-month high on Tuesday as oil prices retreated and investors reassessed the AI-fueled rally that has supported demand for US assets this year, while awaiting fresh clues on the Federal Reserve's interest rate path. "The dollar is retreating as skepticism grows over the strength and sustainability of artificial intelligence-related equity valuations, threatening to curb capital inflows into American financial markets," said Karl Schamotta, chief market strategist at Corpay in Toronto. The dollar further extended losses after New York Fed President John Williams said [USN:FWN45Z0WW TEXT:"he still expects"] one more rate hike this year, but sees no need for further increases in 2027. That left the US dollar index , a measure of the greenback's strength against a basket of six currencies, down 0.37% to 102.18 after reaching 102.61 on Monday, its highest level since April 2025. Markets expect US President Donald Trump to avoid escalation in the Middle East , as a wider conflict could hurt his standing ahead of the midterm elections next month. Trump said last week the [USN:L1N45U0PH TEXT:"US will not attack Iran"] before the elections, and he [USN:L1N45X021 TEXT:"mentioned an energy ceasefire"] between Russia and Ukraine on Sunday. [USN:L1N45Z00X TEXT:"Oil prices fell"] 0.75% to $105.87 per barrel on Tuesday, as traders weighed the prospect of additional Russian diesel supplies. Russia said it can restore diesel exports [USN:S8N45E0D7 TEXT:"beyond levels"] Trump outlined in a deal with Moscow. Beyond energy , analysts said the dollar's recent rally is also being challenged by growing doubts about the artificial intelligence-driven investment story. Investors are now awaiting the release on Wednesday of the US Consumer Price Index for September, which should provide further clues about possible Fed policy tightening. Investors abandoned bets on a Fed rate hike later this month after two policymakers argued for gathering [USN:L6N45N16X TEXT:"more evidence before deciding"] whether further tightening is needed, while Fed Governor Christopher Waller said [USN:L1N45Z0AY TEXT:"inflation expectations remained "well anchored.""] Traders see about an 80% chance that the Fed will leave rates unchanged at its October 27-28 meeting, up from 51% a month ago, while pricing in about 75 basis points of tightening by late 2027, CME Group's FedWatch Tool showed. "We think it’s going to be softish. There’s a bit of headline risk because of the oil prices," said Steven Englander, head of global G10 FX research and North America macro strategy at Standard Chartered Bank in New York. "But some of the factors pushing up core are fading. Tariffs are last year's news." Rising oil prices recently have been supporting the dollar at the expense of currencies such as the euro and yen, which are linked to economies far more dependent than the US on imported oil. EURO REBOUNDS DESPITE GAS PRICES HITTING HIGHS The euro rebounded from a roughly 17-month low on Tuesday despite another jump in gas prices, a key driver of euro zone inflation, while concerns over France's fiscal outlook persisted. It was up 0.40% at $1.1198 after hitting $1.11525 on Monday, its lowest level since May 2025. "There has been a slight narrowing in bond spreads within Europe," said Englander. "We are not at Defcon 1 when it comes to perceptions of French fiscal vulnerability. We have backed off that." Natural gas prices in Europe rose to their highest level since December 2022 and were last at €86.74 per megawatt-hour. The yen strengthened 0.18% to 158.33 against the dollar after Bank of Japan data showed [USN:L4N45Y1EW TEXT:"wholesale prices"] rose 6.8% in the year to September, missing a median market forecast of 7.6% but still enough to justify market fears of higher interest rates. Investors continued to see support from the prospect of further BoJ policy tightening, and the risk of official intervention against excessive currency moves. The euro was last up 0.19% at 177.295 versus the Japanese currency , after hitting 176.25, its lowest level since November 2025. The Australian dollar was at $0.69830, following the release of the [USN:P8N44M01S TEXT:"minutes"] from the Reserve Bank of Australia's September board meeting. The board voted unanimously to raise rates for the fourth time this year.

item.title: World stocks slip as AI spending worries hit chipmakers
item.description: World stocks edged lower on Tuesday as concerns about AI spending weighed on chipmakers and investors looked ahead to more US corporate earnings for clues on whether big technology firms can justify their heavy capital expenditure.
item.dc:creator: Sruthi Shankar, Chibuike Oguh
item.content:encoded: World stocks edged lower on Tuesday as concerns about AI spending [USN:L1N45Z05C TEXT:"weighed on"] chipmakers and investors looked ahead to more US corporate earnings for clues on whether big technology firms can justify their heavy capital expenditure. Brent crude futures also fell as traders assessed developments in the Middle East conflict. Investors have ridden the AI wave in the past four years as massive spending powered corporate profits and economic growth, although worries over concentration risks and whether a payoff will come soon enough have weighed. On Wall Street, all three indexes were lower with industrials, healthcare, financials and technology stocks driving losses. Chip stocks (.SOX) were down more than 1%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average (.DJI) fell 0.31%, the S&P 500 (.SPX) fell 0.10% and the Nasdaq Composite (.IXIC) fell 0.26%. The pan-European STOXX 600 (.STOXX) index fell 0.1%. The MSCI's main world stocks index (.MIWD00000PUS) dipped 0.25%. "The AI trade has been driving the market for the first part of the year up until the third quarter and usually the Nvidias and AMDs trade down ahead of the hyperscalers' earnings announcements because of the uncertainty with regards to the capital spending cycle," said Gerry Sparrow, president and portfolio manager at Sparrow Capital Management. Reported progress by Chinese memory chip maker CXMT has fueled concerns about increased competition from China's AI players, while Broadcom (AVGO.O) CEO Hock Tan [USN:L1N45Z07U TEXT:"likened"] some of the flows into the broader AI sector to "casino gambling." EARNINGS KICK-OFF Investors are turning their eyes to the US quarterly season, which kicked off with results from big [USN:L1N45R0GT TEXT:"banks"]. [USN:L4N45Z0W2 TEXT:"JPMorgan Chase"] (JPM.N) inched up 0.14% after it reported a profit increase in the third quarter, driven by investment banking and trading performances. [USN:L4N45Z0VX TEXT:"Wells Fargo"] (WFC.N) dropped 2.1%, while [USN:L4N45Z111 TEXT:"Goldman Sachs"] (GS.N) climbed 0.54% after their results. AI heavyweights Alphabet (GOOGL.O) , Amazon.com (AMZN.O) , Meta Platforms (META.O) and Nvidia (NVDA.O) are yet to report their quarterly results. "Until we get clarity on hyperscaler capital spending and revenue on the AI trade, you're going to see some very mixed results on the benchmarks: Dow, S&P 500 and the Nasdaq," Sparrow said. BOND YIELDS EASE The benchmark 10-year yield fell 2.29 basis points to 5.22%, inching away from the 24-year high of 5.364% it hit last week. A toxic mix of inflationary pressure from elevated energy prices and worries about ballooning government debt has triggered several bond selloffs in recent weeks, pushing borrowing costs to multi-decade highs across the globe. Traders are awaiting US inflation data on Wednesday for clues on the Federal Reserve's policy path. They are pricing in an 80.6% chance that it holds rates steady later this month, up from 51% a month earlier, the CME FedWatch tool showed. Oil prices eased as traders assessed supply risks from attacks on Saudi Arabia while weighing the prospect of additional diesel supplies from Russia . Brent crude futures dipped 0.9% to $105.69 per barrel. The dollar eased from 18-month highs, along with a drop in yields and oil prices. The euro was last up 0.44% at $1.1202, while the Japanese yen was at 158.27 per dollar, up 0.22%. The dollar index , which measures the greenback against a basket of currencies including the yen and the euro, fell 0.37%.

item.title: Oil prices settle mixed, focus on US-Russia diesel deal, Saudi Yemen attacks
item.description: Oil prices were mixed on Tuesday as hopes the US-Russia diesel deal could free up more supplies from Moscow offset attacks in Saudi Arabia and Yemen that could result in additional supply disruptions.
item.dc:creator: Scott Disavino
item.content:encoded: Oil prices were mixed on Tuesday as hopes the US-Russia diesel deal could free up more supplies from Moscow offset attacks in Saudi Arabia and Yemen that could result in additional supply disruptions. Brent futures settled at $105.69 per barrel, down 96 cents, or 0.9% from Monday, which was its highest settlement since September 15. US West Texas Intermediate crude futures rose 40 cents, or 0.4%, to settle at $94.14, the highest close for WTI since September 24. WTI futures for calendar 2027 rose to a record high for a 12th day in a row, reaching $84 per barrel. On Monday, Brent futures for calendar 2027 rose to a record high for a fourth day in a row, reaching $90. The Kremlin said it did not see any direct link between a deal on [USN:L1N45Z0B7 TEXT:"exporting Russian diesel"] to the US and Moscow's stance on the Ukraine peace talks. It was commenting on a Reuters source-based story, which reported that [USN:L4N45Y0AR TEXT:"US President Donald Trump's"] envoys had told Ukrainian officials on Friday that the deal to allow Russian diesel exports was part of an attempt to draw Russia back into negotiations over a possible peace settlement in Ukraine. Russia was the world's third-biggest crude oil producer behind the US and Saudi Arabia in 2025, according to US energy data. Sanctions designed to keep Russian energy out of global markets have helped support oil prices since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022. Any deal to end the Russia-Ukraine war could allow Russia to export more energy. [USN:L1N45Z0GP TEXT:"Ukraine received no warning"] from Western partners before a Russian missile attack on its capital, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Tuesday. Trump said Washington was still sharing intelligence even as he pressures Kyiv to halt attacks on Russian refineries. [USN:S0N435010 TEXT:"Trump"] said Russian diesel was for the rest of the world, not the US. In a sign the market is uncertain about Trump's diesel deal with Russia, US diesel futures were trading up around 5% on Tuesday. Diesel prices rose to record highs in many parts of the world in recent weeks due to global supply disruptions linked to Ukraine's attacks on Russian energy infrastructure and Iran's attacks on Middle East energy infrastructure. Elsewhere, the [USN:L8N45Z17L TEXT:"UK's domestic spy chief"] said on Tuesday that Russia and Iran were stepping up hybrid warfare campaigns in Britain. MIDDLE EAST ATTACKS [USN:L1N45Z0HH TEXT:"Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis"] said Saudi Arabia was attacking the Yemeni capital Sanaa on Tuesday after a Saudi-led coalition warned civilians to stay away from an oil depot on the city outskirts, part of a rapidly escalating war between the sides. Concerns over the vulnerability of Gulf energy infrastructure and shipping lanes remained in focus after Iran-aligned Houthis [USN:L6N45Y0C1 TEXT:"struck Riyadh's international airport"] over the weekend, while [USN:L1N45T0HL TEXT:"tanker attacks"] were [USN:S8N44X01M TEXT:"reported"] near the Strait of Hormuz. Loud booms were heard in the vicinity of [USN:S8N44Y01P TEXT:"Saudi Aramco's headquarters"] in Dhahran, six sources told Reuters. [USN:L1N45Z0S4 TEXT:"Trump"] on Tuesday accused Yemen's Houthi militants of deliberately trying to drive up oil prices ahead of the US midterm elections and warned that he would "never forget" their attacks on Saudi Arabia, amid a widening regional conflict fueled by the US war with Iran. Despite ongoing disruptions of shipments through the Strait of Hormuz during the Iran war, however, oil producer group OPEC+ posted a sharp gain in production in September, the [USN:L6N45Z0RG TEXT:"Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries"] (OPEC) said on Tuesday, driven by an increase from Saudi Arabia. About 20% of global oil supplies passed through the Strait of Hormuz before the US and Israel attacked Iran in February. OPEC+ includes OPEC and allies like Russia. OPEC also lowered its forecast for 2026 oil demand growth for a sixth straight month, and raised its forecast for next year, citing the need for the world to rebuild inventories depleted by the Iran war.

item.title: Pope Leo diagnosed with cancer as doctors remove part of lung, Vatican says
item.description: Pope Leo was diagnosed with lung cancer after surgeons removed a part of his right lung on Tuesday, the Vatican said in a medical bulletin, marking a significant health setback for the 71-year-old pontiff.
item.dc:creator: Joshua McElwee, Matteo Negri
item.content:encoded: Pope Leo was diagnosed with lung cancer after surgeons removed a part of his right lung on Tuesday, the Vatican said in a medical bulletin, marking a significant health setback for the 71-year-old pontiff. The pope has adenocarcinoma, a common form of lung cancer, with tissue tests conducted during the operation confirming what doctors had suspected from preparatory examinations, the bulletin said. Leo was admitted to Rome's Gemelli hospital on Tuesday for surgery to remove the growth that doctors had discovered in a recent health checkup. The Vatican had said earlier on Tuesday evening that the operation had been successful before providing a more detailed update from the pope's lead surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora, and his personal physician, Dr. Luigi Carbone. "In order to make the procedure curative, the lower lobe of the right lung was removed using a video-assisted technique," the medical update said, making clear that the aim was to eliminate all cancerous tissue. Human lungs have five lobes -- three in the right lung and two in the left. Medical experts said that in order to assess the pope's case they would need to know the size of the tumour removed from him and whether the cancer had spread to his lymph nodes, information the Vatican did not immediately provide. "While we have the diagnosis, we do not yet have the stage. This is critical to prognosis and treatment," said Dr. Stephen Liu, a lung cancer expert at Georgetown University in Washington and division chief of hematology-oncology at MedStar Georgetown University Hospital. "If this is a small lung cancer with no lymph nodes involved, surgery itself is likely to be curative," he told Reuters. "But if final analysis reveals a greater extent of cancer involvement, this indicates a poorer prognosis." RESTING IN HIS HOSPITAL ROOM Tuesday's surgery lasted about 90 minutes and was successful with no complications, the Vatican said. The pope has woken up normally and is resting in his hospital room. Leo left the Vatican ahead of the surgery shortly before 1 p.m. (1100 GMT) in Rome and was seen waving from the back of a black SUV as his convoy drove about 9 km (5.6 miles) north of the Vatican to the Gemelli. Upon arrival at the hospital, Leo shook hands with several officials, walked in front of a waiting crowd of well-wishers, some of whom shouted 'Auguri' (best wishes), and headed in via the main entrance. The Vatican said earlier this week that the pope was expected to recover in hospital for about a week. All his public events have been cancelled until October 20. Leo, elected by the world's cardinals in May 2025, is relatively young for a Church leader. He enjoys sports, including tennis, and is not known to be a smoker or to have had recent health issues. The late Pope Francis, Leo's predecessor, was hospitalised several times as he grew frail in his later years. He died aged 88 in April 2025. Leo, who spoke in [USN:L1N45Y081 TEXT:"a firm, clear voice"] at his only public event on Monday, keeps a very busy schedule. He is due to make an 11-day tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from November 6 to 17, but it was clear if this trip would still go ahead. TYPHOID FEVER The pope is the ultimate earthly authority for the world's 1.4 billion Catholics and does not have a deputy who steps in when he is sick. When a pope is incapacitated, the business of the Vatican's vast bureaucracy carries on as usual, holding off on any decisions that require papal approval. Leo, born in Chicago in 1955 as Robert Prevost, served for decades as a missionary and bishop in Peru before becoming pope. In 1985, when he was a young priest, he came down with typhoid fever in Chulucanas, Peru and was hospitalised. He recounted the experience in his only major interview given as pope, in a book for Penguin Peru. Leo said the pain was so bad that he asked God to die rather than continue suffering. He took his survival as a sign from God that "We need you here (on Earth)," he said. "I never looked back," said Leo.

item.title: Russian strike on Kyiv residential building kills two, injures at least nine, officials say
item.description: A Russian strike on a high-rise residential building in a suburb of the Ukrainian capital Kyiv killed two people and injured at least nine, while attacks in other Ukrainian regions killed at least six people, officials said on Monday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: A Russian strike on a high-rise residential building in a suburb of the Ukrainian capital Kyiv killed two people and injured at least nine, while attacks in other Ukrainian regions killed at least six people, officials said on Monday. President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, writing on Telegram, said two people died in the evening strike on the 25-story residence in the Darnitskyi district. Prosecutors said one body was found in a car next to the building. Zelenskiy said nine people were injured in the incident. Pictures posted on unofficial Telegram channels showed parts of an apartment building ablaze. In Kharkiv, Ukraine's second-largest city in the northeast, Mayor Ihor Terekhov reported serious shelling of city districts, with five people injured in the collapse of an entrance to an apartment building. He said residents could still be trapped beneath rubble. Further south in Kharkiv region, officials said one person was killed in a drone attack in the town of Lozova. Regional officials said Russian shelling killed at least three people in a village near Kramatorsk, one of Ukraine's "fortress cities" in eastern Donetsk region that Russian forces have set their sights on in their slow advance westward. In the region surrounding Kyiv, one person was killed in an attack near the town of Fastiv, southwest of the capital, and one person was killed in the southeastern city of Dnipro. Russian attacks on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities, previously conducted chiefly at night, now disrupt daily life virtually around the clock.

item.title: The races that will decide control of the US Senate
item.description: Republicans hold a 53-47 majority in the US Senate, where Democrats would need to flip at least two seats in states that President Donald Trump carried by double digits in 2024 to win a majority in November's midterm elections. But as Election Day nears, Democrats have a real chance at flipping the chamber, something that was considered a long shot at the beginning of this political cycle.
item.dc:creator: Nolan Mccaskill
item.content:encoded: Republicans hold a 53-47 majority in the US Senate, where Democrats would need to flip at least two seats in states that President Donald Trump carried by double digits in 2024 to win a majority in November's midterm elections . But as Election Day nears, Democrats have a real chance at flipping the chamber, something that was considered a long shot at the beginning of this political cycle. Here are the races that will determine control of the Senate: GEORGIA Democrats' top priority is to hold the seats they already have. That means protecting US Senator Jon Ossoff in Georgia and helping progressive Abdul El-Sayed hold an open seat in Michigan. Trump won Georgia by 2 percentage points in 2024 and Michigan by 1 point. Ossoff has been a juggernaut fundraiser, raising $98 million through June 30. He entered July with nearly $43 million on hand. His opponent, US Representative Mike Collins, has raised only $7.4 million and reported $2.1 million on hand. Campaigns are required to file their quarterly fundraising reports this week, which will show how much they've raised between July and September and how much they had on hand entering October. Recent polls show Ossoff, a potential 2028 presidential candidate, with a double-digit lead over Collins. Republicans have outspent Democrats $17 million to $15 million, but Ossoff's campaign funds may be too much for Collins to overcome. MICHIGAN The [USN:L1N4420RK TEXT:"Democratic establishment didn't get its pick"] in Michigan . But embracing a progressive outsider is key to Democrats' strategy to flip control of the Senate. A Democratic loss in Michigan would require the party to flip five Republican-held seats to win a majority. El-Sayed narrowly defeated the establishment favorite in moderate US Representative Haley Stevens during the primary, putting him on a collision course with former US Representative Mike Rogers in what could be the tightest race for a Democratic-held Senate seat this cycle. Rogers released a 30-second ad last week in which he said Canada is not America's enemy, distancing himself from the president and his tariffs. "We need to end this tariff war," a narrator says. "Now!" Former Vice President Kamala Harris has campaigned with El-Sayed, and former President Barack Obama is set to rally with him later this month. The latest batch of polls show El-Sayed leading by between 1 and 7 points. Republicans have spent $86 million in Michigan's Senate race, more than double Democrats' $41 million. NEW HAMPSHIRE Democrats are defending another open seat in New Hampshire , though this is a state Harris won by nearly 3 points in 2024. Democratic US Representative Chris Pappas is running against former US Senator John Sununu, who was ousted by Democrat Jeanne Shaheen in 2008. Shaheen is retiring. Pappas has raised $15 million to Sununu's $4 million. The Democratic congressman also has a $1 million cash advantage over Sununu. But Republicans have helped close the gap for Sununu, whose brother Chris was governor until his term ended last year and whose father — also named John — was a former governor and White House chief of staff for President George H.W. Bush. Republicans have outspent Democrats in this race, $25 million to $12 million. Pappas has maintained a consistent polling lead of 5 to 8 points in recent surveys. MAINE Democrats' top offensive opportunity is in Maine , the lone state where a Republican incumbent is up for reelection in a state Harris won. Harris carried Maine by nearly 7 points in 2024. Senator Susan Collins has routinely distanced herself from Trump and declined to appear in the state with him or Vice President JD Vance. During a debate last week, Collins — who voted to convict Trump after he was impeached following the January 6 insurrection — acknowledged that she isn't the president's favorite senator and said he won't be coming to Maine. But she did help Republicans pass their One Big Beautiful Bill despite voting against its final passage, and Democrats hope voters will hold her accountable for helping confirm Brett Kavanaugh to the US Supreme Court, which led to the overturning of a federal right to abortion. Democrats, however, have their own drama. Maine [USN:L1N42G0S1 TEXT:"Democrats nominated progressive oysterman Graham Platner"], who was [USN:L6N43A0RY TEXT:"pressured into withdrawing"] following sexual assault allegations, forcing the state party to stage a truncated process to name a new nominee. Platner has denied the allegations. Former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson, another progressive, [USN:L6N43P103 TEXT:"emerged as Platner's replacement"]. But he began his Senate campaign this summer with no money. While Platner had outraised Collins, who chairs the Senate's Appropriations Committee, even he significantly trailed her $11 million in cash. Republicans have poured more than $50 million into Maine to reelect Collins, nearly double Democrats' $26 million. But the latest polls show Jackson leading by 4 points. NORTH CAROLINA Republicans appear to have conceded North Carolina , where a top Republican super PAC has diverted resources to Kansas, a state that wasn't considered to be in play until recently. US Senator Thom Tillis, a Republican Trump critic, did not seek reelection. Democrats landed a top recruit for the open seat in former North Carolina Governor Roy Cooper, while Republicans fielded former Republican National Committee Chair Michael Whatley. Like many Democratic candidates, Cooper has dwarfed his opponent in fundraising, raising $35 million with $21 million on hand. Whatley has brought in $11 million and reported $3.5 million in cash. Republicans' $45 million in spending is almost $20 million more than Democrats'. Yet Cooper has led in polls all through September and into October, some by double digits. Trump won North Carolina by 3 points in 2024. OHIO Ohio is one of four battleground states Trump won by double digits in 2024. Democrats need to win at least two such states to win control of the Senate. The Democratic nominee is former US Senator Sherrod Brown, who was ousted by Republican US Senator Bernie Moreno last cycle. This time, Brown faces US Senator Jon Husted, who was appointed to the Senate to replace Vance when he left office for the White House. The winner of the special election will serve the remainder of Vance's term, which expires in January 2029. Brown has brought in $39 million and had $16 million in the bank. Husted has raised $14 million with $9 million banked. The race has become one of the most expensive Senate contests in the nation, with upwards of $200 million in outside spending. Republicans alone are responsible for $143 million. Both candidates have led in recent polls of this toss-up race. ALASKA Trump will rally on Tuesday in Alaska , a state he won by 13 points in 2024. It's also another double-digit Trump state that Republicans could lose. US Senator Dan Sullivan, the Republican incumbent, is running against former US Representative Mary Peltola. Alaska has ranked-choice voting, a process in which voters rank their top picks rather than choosing a single candidate.
